title: How do you use the 4Ps of marketing in a product launch case?
description: The 4Ps (marketing mix) for case interviews. The "What to offer" branch of a product launch. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: Use the 4Ps (product, price, place and promotion) to design the offer once you know who the customer is: decide what to sell, what to charge, where to sell it and how to tell people about it. It belongs in the "what to offer" branch of a launch plan, not at the start of a case about whether to launch.
body:
When it helps

The 4Ps, popularised by the marketing professor E. Jerome McCarthy in 1960, are a checklist for the marketing mix. In a case, they fit the "what to offer" branch of a product launch, after you have chosen the target customer. If the interviewer asks whether to launch, start with demand, economics and the client's ability to win, using the market entry structure.

The checklist

Product

  • Features
  • Range and pack sizes
  • Quality

Price

  • Level against alternatives
  • Discounts
  • Tiers

Place

  • Channels
  • Coverage and shelf access

Promotion

  • Advertising and social media
  • Sales force
  • Sampling and offers

An example: an energy drink for students

A drinks company is launching a low-sugar energy drink for university students. Product: flavours students like, in a can that fits a bag. Price: close to the big brands, perhaps with a multipack deal. Place: campus shops, supermarkets near universities, delivery apps. Promotion: sampling at freshers' fairs and social media. Every answer depends on knowing the customer first, which is why the 4Ps come second.

Check the Ps add up to a business

The four Ps are linked. Price and place together decide how much the client keeps per unit. Take an illustrative protein bar sold in supermarkets:

  • It retails at $2.00 and the retailer keeps 30% of the selling price, so the maker receives $2.00 × 70% = $1.40.
  • Production and logistics cost $0.90, so contribution is $1.40 − $0.90 = $0.50 a bar.
  • Launch spending (listing fees, sampling, advertising) is $500,000, so the maker needs $500,000 ÷ $0.50 = 1 million bars just to cover it.

That changes the plan. A million bars needs wide distribution and repeat buyers, so place and product taste matter as much as clever promotion. It also shows why a small price change matters: each 10 cents of retail price is worth 7 cents to the maker, 14% of its $0.50 contribution.

How it sounds in an interview

"Once we know the customer is students, I'd plan the launch around product, price, place and promotion, starting with where they actually buy drinks, because that decides both our reach and how much margin the retailer takes."

The weak version lists the four words with generic points under each ("good quality, competitive price, many channels, strong marketing") that would fit any product.

Common mistakes

  • Starting with the 4Ps before choosing the customer.
  • Treating each P on its own, when price and channel together decide the margin.
  • Spending the whole answer on promotion. Availability and repeat purchase usually matter more.

Practise it

1. In the bar example, the maker raises the retail price to $2.50 and the retailer still keeps 30%. How many bars cover the $500,000 launch spend now?

Show the answer

The maker receives $2.50 × 70% = $1.75, so contribution is $1.75 − $0.90 = $0.85. Bars needed: $500,000 ÷ $0.85 ≈ 590,000. But a higher price may sell fewer bars, so test whether volume holds up before choosing it.

2. Give a one-line 4Ps plan for a premium dog food sold online to busy city owners.

Show the answer

Product: fresh, portioned meals by dog size. Price: a monthly subscription, above supermarket brands. Place: the client's own website with home delivery. Promotion: vet partnerships and a discounted first box to drive trial.
